questions.q: An ArrayList is full and add is called. Why is add still called O(1) amortised?
o: The array is copied only occasionally, and capacity grows geometrically
It copies the whole array on every single add
It inserts the new element at the front each time
It never needs to resize because lists are unbounded
questions.w: Most adds are a single write; the O(n) copy happens rarely, so the cost averaged over many adds is constant.

questions.q: Why is ArrayList usually faster than LinkedList for traversal in practice?
o: Its elements sit contiguously in memory, so the CPU cache is used well
Every ArrayList operation is O(1)
LinkedList cannot store more than a few elements
ArrayList nodes hold pointers to the next element
questions.w: Contiguous elements mean fewer cache misses and less memory per element. LinkedList nodes are scattered objects with extra pointers.

questions.q: A HashMap key's hashCode changes after it was stored. What happens on lookup?
o: The entry may not be found, because the lookup goes to a different bucket
The map automatically moves the entry to the right bucket
The lookup always throws an exception
Nothing changes, because equals decides the bucket
questions.w: The bucket was chosen from the old hash code. Keys should be immutable, or at least their hash must not change while stored.

questions.q: What does a plain binary search tree degrade into when keys are inserted in sorted order?
o: A chain like a linked list, with O(n) operations
A perfectly balanced tree with O(log n) operations
A hash table with O(1) operations
A heap with the smallest value on top
questions.w: Each new key goes to the right, so the height equals the number of nodes. Red-black trees such as TreeMap rotate to prevent this.

questions.q: Which structure always gives you the smallest element next, in O(log n) per removal?
o: A min-heap, as in PriorityQueue
A HashMap
An ArrayList kept in insertion order
A queue
questions.w: A heap guarantees only the top element, which makes it ideal for top-k and scheduling, but it is not fully sorted.

questions.q: Which traversal finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
o: Breadth-first search with a queue
Depth-first search with a stack
In-order traversal of a tree
Binary search on the node ids
questions.w: BFS visits nodes in order of distance, so the first time it reaches a node is by the fewest edges. DFS does not guarantee this.

questions.q: Which Java class is the best choice for both a stack and a queue?
o: ArrayDeque
Stack
Vector
LinkedList
questions.w: ArrayDeque has O(1) operations at both ends and no synchronisation overhead; Stack and Vector are legacy synchronised classes.

questions.q: How can you build an LRU cache with O(1) get and put?
o: A hash map combined with a doubly linked list ordered by recent use
A sorted array searched with binary search
A single ArrayList that is scanned on every get
A TreeMap keyed by the value stored
questions.w: The map gives O(1) lookup and the list moves an entry to the front and evicts from the tail in O(1). LinkedHashMap with access order does this.
